rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3.1-3.4 - own modeling chain (Tetis hydrological model, 5 GCM-RCMs, 2 RCPs, 12 parameterizations, 2 irrigation scenarios) producing 240 simulations. Q2: Section 3.2.3 - model calibrated/evaluated against observed ETa, groundwater levels in four wells and plot-scale soil moisture (1994-2015) in the study area; Section 4.3.2 and Figures 3-4 - simulated mean monthly recharge in control period 14.3 mm under drip vs 19.1 mm under flood; Conclusion 2 - recharge is higher in flood irrigation than in drip irrigation. Q4: Sections 2 and 3.2.1 - irrigation volumes of ~630 mm/yr flood vs ~490 mm/yr drip used as input, model simulates soil water storages, wet/dry soil surface fraction (53% wetted), ETa and recharge from the lower soil storage; Section 4.2 - seasonal recharge differences explained by interplay of precipitation, irrigation and ETa. Q6: Section 2 and Figure 1 - 913 km2 study area with 68 irrigation sectors (419 km2), results aggregated at sector and regional scale. Q8: Section 5.3 - farmer behaviour (cropping, pumping) not considered, irrigation schedules held constant, CO2/vegetation feedbacks ignored, static FAO crop coefficient approach; Section 5.2 - prediction uncertainties in magnitude and sign. Q9: Figures 3-5 - ranges across five climate models and boxplots of 60 values (12 parameterizations x 5 GCM-RCMs); Section 5.2 compares spread from climate models vs parameter sets.
rows.notes: Evidence is model-based only (one method), so no triangulation. Single region, single dominant crop (citrus), loam/clay-loam soils, so not representative. Business-as-usual irrigation volumes are stated as an assumption/limitation rather than as a required condition, so Q7 is no. Seasonal reversal (drip recharge higher outside the flood-irrigation season) is reported but as variation, not a requirement.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3.1-3.4 - own hydrological model runs under climate projections. Q2: Section 3.2.3 - model evaluated against observed ETa, groundwater wells and soil moisture in the study area; Section 4.3.1.1 and Figure 5 - significant mean recharge reductions under RCP 8.5 more pronounced in drip (-6.6% near-term, -9.3% mid-term) than flood (-2.4%, -7.3%); Section 4.4 and Figure 9 - planned transformation to 85% drip enhances the negative recharge trend (5.1-7.0 mm/yr), 100% drip would cut annual recharge by 31-35 mm. Q4: Sections 3.2.1 and 4.3.1.1 - model simulates precipitation changes, soil water storage, ETa and recharge; trends in mean recharge follow precipitation declines (-6.5% to -6.6% mid-term). Q6: Section 2, Figure 1, Section 4.4 - regional study area of 913 km2 with 68 irrigation sectors, transformation effects reported for the whole region. Q8: Section 5.3 - farmer behaviour not considered, constant irrigation schedules, no vegetation/CO2 feedback, static crop coefficients; Section 5.2 - uncertainty in magnitude and sign of change. Q9: Figures 3-7 - ranges across five climate models, boxplots of 60 values from 12 parameterizations x 5 GCM-RCMs; Section 5.2 attributes most spread to climate models.
rows.notes: Model-only evidence (no independent method). One region and crop. Significant recharge declines only under RCP 8.5 are reported as a scenario difference, not stated as a requirement, so Q7 is no. Results assume unchanged future irrigation volumes.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a regional hydrological modeling study (Tetis) calibrated against observed ETa, groundwater levels and soil moisture; projections for 2020-2074 are not themselves verifiable but the model was checked against observations of the real system.
